```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
```


## Question 1

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```

```{r}
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)
```

```{r}
missing_summary =
  ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    missing_prcp = mean(is.na(prcp)) * 100,
    missing_snow = mean(is.na(snow)) * 100,
    missing_snwd = mean(is.na(snwd)) * 100,
    missing_tmax = mean(is.na(tmax)) * 100,
    missing_tmin = mean(is.na(tmin)) * 100
  )

missing_summary |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```


The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, including weather station ID, date, precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

Missing data are a substantial issue in this dataset. Precipitation has the lowest percentage of missing values (`r round(missing_summary$missing_prcp, 2)`%), followed by snowfall (`r round(missing_summary$missing_snow, 2)`%) and snow depth (`r round(missing_summary$missing_snwd, 2)`%). Maximum and minimum temperatures have the highest missing percentages, both at `r round(missing_summary$missing_tmax, 2)`%.


```{r}
ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```

The original maximum and minimum temperatures (`tmax` and `tmin`) were recorded in tenths of degrees Celsius, but precipitation (`prcp`) was recorded in tenths of millimeters. Therefore, I divided these variables by 10 to convert them into degrees Celsius and millimeters. Snowfall (`snow`) was already measured in millimeters, so no conversion was needed.

```{r}
snow_summary =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

snow_summary |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable()
```


The most commonly observed snowfall value is `r snow_summary$snow[1]` mm, which occurrs `r snow_summary$n[1]` times. This is expected because most days do not experience snowfall.

Other frequently observed values include `r snow_summary$snow[2]`, `r snow_summary$snow[3]`, `r snow_summary$snow[4]`, and `r snow_summary$snow[5]` mm. These values are approximately equivalent to common fractions or multiples of an inch. It suggests that the observed frequencies may reflect measurement conventions and rounding when converting from inches to millimeters.


```{r}
temp_summary =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax))
```

```{r}
temp_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, 10)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month,
           labeller = as_labeller(c(`1` = "January", `7` = "July"))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```



The plot shows a clear seasonal difference in average maximum temperatures between January and July. January temperatures are generally much lower and more variable. July temperatures are higher and more concentrated. There is some variation across years, but no obvious long-term trend.

A few potential outliers are visible in both months, particularly unusually low average temperatures in January and July. These values may reflect extreme weather conditions or incomplete observations and would require further investigation.


```{r}
ggp_temp =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggp_snow =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 5) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```


```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=14}
combined_plot =
  (ggp_temp / ggp_snow) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Temperature and Snowfall in New York",
    tag_levels = "A"
  )

combined_plot
```
Panel A: Maximum vs Minimum Temperature:

The plot shows a clear positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperatures. As minimum temperature increases, maximum temperature generally increases as well. There are few potential outliers at unusually high or low temperatures. A hexbin plot is more appropriate than a scatterplot for this large dataset because it reduces overplotting and makes the concentration of observations easier to see.

Panel B: Distribution of Snowfall by Year:

My code focuses on snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 mm. So I excluded days with no snowfall and observations with snowfall of 100 mm or more.

The distributions of snowfall are relatively consistent across years. There are no obvious long-term changes in their overall shapes. Smaller snowfall amounts are more common, and larger snowfall amounts occur less frequently. Several peaks appear at similar snowfall values across years, which may reflect measurement conventions and rounding when converting snowfall measurements from inches to millimeters.


## Question 2

```{r,message=FALSE}
demographic_df = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)

accelerometer_df = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```


```{r}
demographic_clean =
  demographic_df |>
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(BMI),
    !is.na(education)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    SEQN = as.character(SEQN),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female"),
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

```

```{r}
accelerometer_long =
  accelerometer_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    SEQN = as.character(SEQN),
    minute = as.numeric(
      stringr::str_remove(minute, "min")
    )
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_df =
  accelerometer_long |>
  inner_join(
    demographic_clean,
    by = "SEQN"
  )
```

```{r}
education_sex_df =
  demographic_clean |>
  group_by(education, sex) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
education_sex_df |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

After excluding participants younger than 21 or with missing demographic information, `r nrow(demographic_clean)` participants remained from the original `r nrow(demographic_df)` participants. The largest education group was more than high school, with `r sum(demographic_clean$education == "More than high school")` participants. The numbers of men and women were relatively balanced in the less than high school and more than high school groups. However, in the high school equivalent group, there were more men (`r sum(demographic_clean$education == "High school equivalent" & demographic_clean$sex == "Male")`) than women (`r sum(demographic_clean$education == "High school equivalent" & demographic_clean$sex == "Female")`).

```{r}
ggplot(demographic_clean,
  aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The age distributions vary across education levels and sex. Participants with less than a high school education generally have higher median ages, which are around 60 years for both men and women. In the high school equivalent group, women have a higher median age than men. Participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger, with median ages in the early to mid-40s for both sexes. Overall, the results suggest that age distributions differ across education categories, although there is considerable overlap between groups.


```{r}
daily_activity_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(
  daily_activity_df,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The scatterplots suggest that total daily activity generally decreases with age, particularly among older participants. Female participants tend to have slightly higher activity levels than male participants in several age ranges, but this pattern is not consistent across all education groups. The high school equivalent group shows more fluctuations in activity trends. The more than high school group exhibits relatively stable activity levels through middle age, followed by a decline among older participants. Overall, the results suggest an association between age and daily activity, with some differences by sex and education level.

```{r, message=FALSE}
activity_time_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarise(
    mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(
  activity_time_df,
  aes(x = hour, y = mean_MIMS, color = sex)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, 4)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Education and Sex",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Mean Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The 24-hour activity patterns show a clear daily cycle across all three education levels. Activity levels are lowest during the early morning hours, increase rapidly after approximately 6 AM, remain relatively high throughout the day, and decline in the evening. Female participants generally have higher mean activity levels than male participants during daytime hours. Participants with less than a high school education show a pronounced peak around midday. Those with a high school equivalent education exhibit relatively lower daytime activity levels. Overall, the results suggest similar daily activity patterns across education groups, with some differences in activity intensity by sex and education level.


## Question 3

```{r,message=FALSE}
jan_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip")

july_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip")

jan_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip")

july_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip")
```

```{r}
citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
    july_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
    jan_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
    july_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
  )
```

```{r}
citibike_clean =
  citibike_df |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )
```

The cleaned Citi Bike dataset contains `r nrow(citibike_clean)` rides from January and July of `r paste(sort(unique(citibike_clean$year)), collapse = " and ")`, with `r ncol(citibike_clean)` variables describing ride characteristics。 The dataset includes bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting and ending stations, membership status, year, and month. Categorical variables were converted to factors with appropriate ordering. There are `r sum(is.na(citibike_clean$start_station_name))` missing starting station names and `r sum(is.na(citibike_clean$end_station_name))` missing ending station names, and all other variables have no missing values. Ride durations range from approximately `r round(min(citibike_clean$duration), 0)` to `r round(max(citibike_clean$duration), 0)` minutes, with a median of `r round(median(citibike_clean$duration), 2)` minutes. All rides were retained for the analysis, except that records with missing starting station names were excluded when ranking starting stations.

```{r}
ride_count_df =
  citibike_clean |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarise(
    n_rides = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ride_count_df |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n_rides
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Citi Bike members accounted for more rides than casual riders in all four months. In both 2020 and 2024, July had more rides than January, which suggests a seasonal pattern in bike usage. The number of rides was also higher in 2024 than in 2020 for both months. July 2024 had the highest number of rides, while January 2020 had the lowest. 

```{r}
top_stations_df =
  citibike_clean |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    name = "n_rides"
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = n_rides,
    n = 5,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

top_stations_df |>
  knitr::kable()
```

In July 2024, Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station, followed by University Pl & E 14 St and W 21 St & 6 Ave. The five most popular stations had relatively similar ride counts, ranging from 146 to 163 rides.


```{r}
median_duration_df =
  citibike_clean |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(
    median_duration = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  median_duration_df,
  aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = month,
    group = month
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```


Median ride duration was consistently higher in July than in January for both 2020 and 2024. Rides also tended to last longer on weekends. In July 2020, median duration reached approximately 16.5 minutes on Saturday and Sunday. Overall, median ride durations were higher in 2020 than in 2024, with the largest difference occurring in July. These patterns suggest that ride duration varies by season, day of the week, and year.

```{r}
citibike_2024 =
  citibike_clean |>
  filter(year == 2024)
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  citibike_2024,
  aes(
    x = member_casual,
    y = duration,
    fill = rideable_type
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type in 2024",
    x = "Membership Status",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  citibike_2024,
  aes(
    x = member_casual,
    y = duration,
    fill = rideable_type
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type in 2024",
    x = "Membership Status",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

I created two different plots. For the second plot, the y-axis is limited to 0–60 minutes for readability; all observations were retained when calculating the boxplots.

The boxplots show differences in ride duration by month, membership status, and bike type. Casual riders generally have longer median ride durations than members, particularly when using classic bikes. Among casual riders, classic bikes have higher median ride durations than electric bikes, while electric bikes have slightly higher medians among members. Ride durations tend to be longer in July than in January. All groups exhibit right-skewed distributions with numerous high-duration outliers. Casual riders using classic bikes also show greater variability in ride duration, as indicated by their wider interquartile ranges.
